title: Perceived smartphone excess can coexist with utility, attempted cutback, and incomplete self-regulation
source_unit: Pew Research Center American Trends Panel smartphone-time and self-regulation survey
geography: United States; 9,750 adults in the American Trends Panel

observations.period: May 26-June 1, 2026; Pew American Trends Panel field period

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the American Trends Panel; item denominators exclude nonresponse and some measures exclude people without smartphones

perceived_excess.unit: percent of adults answering the smartphone-time item saying they spend too much time on their smartphone

near_constant_use.unit: percent reporting smartphone use almost constantly

utility_and_cost.value: 73% said smartphones help them access information, 51% said smartphones help them stay connected, and 41% said smartphone use hurts their sleep; productivity judgments were divided

cutback_attempt.unit: percent saying they tried to cut back in the prior 12 months; among those trying, 25% reported high success, 52% some success, and 23% little or no success

durable_change.unit: missing logged use, notification exposure, work or school obligation, repeated follow-up, platform response, wellbeing change, switching, and non-use outcome

mechanism.value: The same device can supply information and connection while creating perceived time, sleep, and productivity costs; personal self-regulation is therefore attempted within a platform-shaped control surface rather than a simple preference choice

observations.method: Structured extraction from Pew's official survey article and published tables; perceived excess, utility, cutback attempt, self-rated success, and open downstream outcomes are kept separate.
observations.uncertainty: This is a self-reported cross-sectional panel survey, not a device-use log, clinical assessment, causal estimate, or durable follow-up. Content, notifications, work and school obligations, platform identity, privacy choices, and later behavior are not retained.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults in the American Trends Panel, with smartphone ownership and age subgroups varying by item; no individual trajectory is followed.
observations.counterinterpretation: Frequent or near-constant use is not identical to harmful dependence, and a failed cutback may reflect social, economic, work, or school necessity rather than simple lack of willpower.

boundary: This record establishes a bounded self-reported chain from smartphone utility and perceived excess through attempted self-regulation and incomplete success. It does not establish addiction, logged behavior, platform causality, clinical harm, or later switching, non-use, or wellbeing recovery.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The hash covers the compact project event ledger derived from Pew's published survey results; respondent-level panel data and device logs are not retained.
